extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, actors, theatre-managers, critics and theatre-going public in early 18th-century England
extracted.subtask_description: Practical critical guidance on composing, staging, and performing tragedies: how to move pity and terror, when to use stage effects, costume and prop practices, and how to avoid common theatrical absurdities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raise terror and pity by sentiments and expressions, not by dresses and decorations
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle has observed, That ordinary Writers in Tragedy endeavour to raise Terror and Pity in their Audience, not by proper Sentiments and Expressions, but by the Dresses and Decorations of the Stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic insists the reader's imagination should be inflamed by dignity of thought and sublimity of expression rather than by costume or scenery. Mechanical artifices may work on the vulgar but the discerning audience sees through them. Examples: thunder/lightning and other stage tricks can assist, but should not substitute for strong writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive costume ornaments that distract the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary Method of making an Hero, is to clap a huge Plume of Feathers upon his Head... the Princess generally receives her Grandeur from those additional Incumbrances that fall into her Tail: I mean the broad sweeping Train that follows her in all her Motions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large plumes and sweeping trains force actors into constrained physicality (holding necks stiff, relying on pages to manage trains) and draw the audience's attention away from speech and feeling. Costuming should not impede natural action or make performers look ridiculous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell large-scale incidents (armies, battles) rather than attempting to represent them onstage
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible for the Reader's Imagination to multiply twenty Men into such prodigious Multitudes... Incidents of such a Nature should be told, not represented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scenes with vast numbers or large-scale events are better related through speech and description; onstage attempts (two or three hundred thousand soldiers in a small room) are implausible and diminish effect. The French example is commended where kings appear unattended and armies are left offstage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ban the noisy military stage effects (drums, trumpets, huzzas)
rubrics_metrics.description: I should likewise be glad if we imitated the French in banishing from our Stage the Noise of Drums, Trumpets, and Huzzas; which is sometimes so very great, that when there is a Battle in the Hay-Market Theatre, one may hear it as far as Charing-Cross.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive martial noise is vulgar and overpowers the audience; prefer restraint so that sound does not swamp sentiment or language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use thunder, lightning, bells, and ghosts only as well-introduced aids to the poet
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be a proper Season for these several Terrors; and when they only come in as Aids and Assistances to the Poet, they are not only to be excused, but to be applauded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage effects must be accompanied by suitable sentiments and expressions to be effective. Positive examples: the sounding clock in Venice Preserved and the appearance of the Ghost in Hamlet (prepared for by preceding discourse) are masterfully used.

rubrics_metrics.name: For moving pity, apply theatrical devices judiciously; ensure speech matches gesture
rubrics_metrics.description: For the moving of Pity, our principal Machine is the Handkerchief... All that I would contend for, is, to keep it from being misapplied. In a Word, I would have the Actor's Tongue sympathize with his Eyes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common tragic devices (handkerchiefs, weeping mothers, children) can be effective, but overuse or clumsy amplification (adding children to double distress twice or more) becomes ridiculous in bad hands. Emotional display must be supported by appropriate language and motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid onstage butchering and grotesque displays of blood; prefer offstage handling of murders
rubrics_metrics.description: Among all our Methods of moving Pity or Terror, there is none so absurd and barbarous... than that dreadful butchering of one another, which is so very frequent upon the English Stage. To delight in seeing Men stabbed, poysoned, racked, or impaled, is certainly the Sign of a cruel Temper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The French habit of transacting murders and executions behind the scenes is commended; ancient practice (e.g., Sophocles' Orestes) uses offstage action and heard dialogue to produce stronger affect. If a killing is essential, it often should be related rather than enacted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer dignity of thought and sublimity of expression over stage trappings
rubrics_metrics.description: I would have our Conceptions raised by the Dignity of Thought and Sublimity of Expression, rather than by a Train of Robes or a Plume of Feathers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great characters obtain grandeur from language and idea (e.g., Brutus in Shakespeare) not from outward equipage. Poets should aim to elevate the mind by speech rather than rely on external pomp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge that tailors and painters (scenery and dress) materially affect a play's success
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tailor and the Painter often contribute to the Success of a Tragedy more than the Poet. Scenes affect ordinary Minds as much as Speeches; and our Actors are very sensible, that a well-dressed Play has sometimes brought them as full Audiences, as a well-written one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical acknowledgement that spectacle attracts audiences (the Italian term cited: Fourberia della Scena — the knavery/trickish part of the drama). This is a caution that spectacle can impose upon judgment; authors should be aware of this dynamic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid artificial personal appearance; prefer natural features enlivened by mind
rubrics_metrics.description: There are Women who do not let their Husbands see their Faces till they are married... The British have a lively, animated Aspect; The Picts, tho' never so Beautiful, have dead, uninformed Countenances... As for my Dear, never Man was so Enamour'd as I was of her fair Forehead, Neck, and Arms, as well as the bright Jett of her Hair; but to my great Astonishment, I find they were all the Effects of Art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steele condemns excessive painting and artificial complexions in women as deceptive and offensive in close approach; recommends natural cheerfulness and good humour (exemplified by 'Statira') as the proper way to improve charms. Deceitful artifice in appearance can ruin trust and social relations.
